title: YOU KNOW BIBLE VERSES… BUT DO YOU ACTUALLY KNOW THE GOD WHO WROTE THEM?
paragraphs: YOU KNOW BIBLE VERSES… BUT DO YOU ACTUALLY KNOW THE GOD WHO WROTE THEM?

The most terrifying spiritual tragedy isn't forgetting what Scripture says. It's knowing the words of eternal life while remaining a stranger to the One who gives it. And one day, the difference between knowing about Jesus and truly belonging to Him will matter more than anything else.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every churchgoer uncomfortable.
Not because it was spoken to atheists.
Not because it was directed at people who had never opened a Bible.
But because Jesus spoke it about people who were convinced they knew God.
People who could speak His name.
People who were religiously active.
People who had impressive spiritual accomplishments to point to.
And yet, when the moment of truth arrived, Jesus said something devastating.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not, “I knew you once, but I forgot you.”
Not, “You didn't memorize enough Scripture.”
Not even, “You failed to attend enough religious gatherings.”
“I never knew you.”
Imagine standing before the Lord Jesus Christ with a lifetime of religious activity behind you, only to discover that the relationship you assumed existed was never there.
Imagine remembering every sermon you shared, every worship song you sang, every Bible verse you posted, every argument you won defending Christianity.
And then hearing those words.
“I never knew you.”
That is not a comfortable thought.
It isn't supposed to be.
But before you close this article because it feels too personal, please understand something.
Jesus did not give this warning so that every struggling believer would live in constant terror.
He gave it because religious appearance can deceive us, and because eternity is too important for us to build our confidence on something other than Him.
And perhaps the most merciful thing God can do for someone who has been hiding behind religion is expose the difference between knowing His words and knowing His heart.
Because you can know Bible verses…
And still refuse to surrender the very sin those verses confront.
You can know how to explain grace…
And still secretly believe your performance is what makes God accept you.
You can post about forgiveness…
While nurturing bitterness toward someone who wounded you.
You can speak passionately about holiness…
While protecting a private compromise that nobody in your church knows exists.
You can recognize false teaching in seconds…
And remain painfully blind to the pride growing inside your own heart.
And the frightening part?
Sometimes you can become so skilled at appearing spiritually mature that you stop asking whether you are actually growing closer to Jesus.
People begin asking you for advice.
They admire your biblical knowledge.
They call you strong in the faith.
They assume your private life must be as beautiful as your public words.
And you smile.
Because correcting their impression would require admitting that the person everyone thinks is spiritually healthy has been struggling to pray when nobody is watching.
You know the verse about casting your burdens upon the Lord.
But you haven't honestly told Him how exhausted you are.
You know the verse about confessing your sins.
But there is something you keep renaming as a weakness because calling it sin would require repentance.
You know the verse about loving your enemies.
But you still rehearse imaginary conversations in which the person who hurt you finally suffers enough to understand your pain.
You know the verse about seeking first the kingdom of God.
But your decisions are increasingly controlled by money, recognition, comfort, fear, or the approval of people who cannot save your soul.
And somewhere along the way, Scripture became something you could quote without allowing it to question you.
Something you could use to correct others without letting it correct you.
Something you could carry in your hand while keeping its Author at a distance.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Not because biblical knowledge is bad.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
It is a gift.
It is necessary for Christian maturity.
But knowledge of Scripture was never intended to become a substitute for communion with the God revealed through Scripture.
Jesus Himself confronted this exact problem.
In John 5:39–40, He spoke to people who searched the Scriptures diligently.
These were not casual readers.
They were serious students of the sacred writings.
They knew the history, the commandments, the promises, the prophetic expectations.
Yet Jesus said:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” — John 5:39–40 (KJV)
That passage is almost unbearable when you understand what is happening.
They were studying the writings that testified about the Messiah.
And when the Messiah stood before them, they refused to come to Him.
They had the testimony.
They were rejecting the Person.
They knew the promises.
They were resisting their fulfillment.
They had spent years studying the Scriptures that pointed toward Jesus.
And then they stood face-to-face with Jesus and would not receive Him.
Can you imagine?
Reading the directions to a place for your entire life…
Then refusing to enter when you finally arrive.
Memorizing the description of a physician…
Then rejecting Him when He comes to heal you.
Studying the promises of a Savior…
Then turning away from the Savior Himself.
And before we look down on those people, we should ask whether our own hearts are capable of doing the same thing.
Because it is possible to become so occupied with the language of Christianity that we neglect the living Christ at its center.
The original Greek of John 5:40 makes the personal nature of Jesus' invitation unmistakable.
καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχητε
Kai ou thelete elthein pros me hina zōēn echēte.
“And you are not willing to come to Me so that you may have life.”
Notice the words οὐ θέλετε — ou thelete.
“You are not willing.”
Jesus identifies a refusal of the will.
The problem was not that Scripture had failed to testify.
The problem was that they would not come to the One to whom Scripture testified.
And notice something else.
Jesus did not say, “Come to a more impressive religious reputation.”
He did not say, “Come to a more sophisticated theological vocabulary.”
He said, in essence, Come to Me.
That is where life is found.
Not in your ability to sound Christian.
Not in the number of passages you can recite.
Not in your capacity to win theological arguments.
Life is found in Jesus Christ.
The Scriptures are God's inspired testimony, and through them we are led to know, trust, worship, and obey the Savior they reveal.
That distinction matters.
Because the answer to spiritually empty Bible knowledge is not less Bible.
It is reading the Bible with a heart that genuinely seeks the Lord.
It is allowing the truth you understand to become truth you believe, receive, and live.
It is coming to Christ.
And sometimes that begins with a painfully honest prayer.
“Lord, I know how to talk about You. But have I been walking with You?”
There are people reading this who haven't prayed that honestly in years.
Not because they don't believe in God.
But because honest prayer would expose things they have worked very hard to keep buried.
The marriage that looks fine in photographs but feels cold behind closed doors.
The secret addiction that returns whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
The envy that rises when another person receives the blessing you have begged God to give you.
The spiritual exhaustion hidden beneath the words, “I'm blessed.”
The resentment toward God that you feel ashamed even to admit.
The quiet question you whisper after everyone else has fallen asleep:
“Lord, where are You?”
And perhaps you have become so accustomed to presenting your best self to people that you have started presenting that same carefully edited version of yourself to God.
You approach Him with polished sentences.
Safe confessions.
Acceptable emotions.
You tell Him what sounds spiritually mature.
But you avoid telling Him what is actually happening inside you.
Yet the God of Scripture is not fooled by religious vocabulary.
Psalm 139:1–2 says:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off.” (KJV)
Long before you found the words to explain your struggle, He knew.
Before you confessed your jealousy, He saw it.
Before you admitted your fear, He understood it.
Before you could name the wound you have been carrying since childhood, He knew its depth.
You do not have to inform God of something He has overlooked.
You are invited to bring into the light what He already sees.
And that is why genuine repentance is not about finally convincing God that you are good.
It is about abandoning the exhausting performance of pretending you do not need mercy.
Listen to David after his sin was exposed.
He did not simply recite religious truths to protect his image.
He cried:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10 (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the opening plea is:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא — bera, from the Hebrew root bara, means “create.”
David was not asking God merely to improve his public image.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
He had sinned.
He had tried to conceal what he had done.
He had been confronted.
And now, stripped of his excuses, he was asking God for something deeper than the restoration of his reputation.
He wanted a clean heart.
This is what happens when Scripture moves beyond the surface of our lives.
We stop using biblical truth merely to evaluate other people's failures.
We begin allowing it to expose our own.
We stop asking only, “What does this verse mean?”
We begin asking, “Lord, what must change in me because this is true?”
And when the answer is painful, we do not have to run away from Christ.
We can run toward Him.
Because the Jesus who exposes sin is also the Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
Think about Peter.
Peter knew who Jesus was.
He had walked with Him.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed miracles that generations before him had only dreamed of seeing.
He had even confessed:
“Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” — Matthew 16:16 (KJV)
What a confession.
Theologically true.
Spiritually significant.
And yet, when fear entered the courtyard on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the sound of his own voice.
“I know not the man.” — Matthew 26:72.
Imagine the sickening realization after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering the confidence with which he had promised never to abandon Jesus.
Then remembering what he had just done.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter.
And Peter remembered.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Scripture does not tell us every thought that passed through Peter's mind in that moment.
But we know the weight of what had happened.
The man who had publicly confessed Jesus had publicly denied Him.
The disciple who thought he was strong had discovered how fragile his courage could be.
And if you have ever looked back at something you said, did, watched, concealed, or betrayed and wondered how someone who knows the truth could have fallen so badly…
You may understand something of Peter's grief.
But do not stop reading Peter's story at the courtyard.
Because Jesus did not.
After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples again.
And in John 21, He spoke directly to Peter.
Three times Jesus asked him about his love.
Three times Peter answered.
And Jesus entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The disciple who had denied Him was not beyond the reach of restoration.
But notice what restored Peter.
Not Peter's ability to produce a more impressive religious résumé.
Not his promise that he would never fail again.
Not his attempt to erase the past.
It was the risen Christ, who graciously confronted him and called him forward.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin is insignificant.
Not that betrayal is harmless.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and His grace is sufficient to forgive, restore, and transform those who turn to Him in faith.
Your worst failure does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
And if you have been treating your spiritual failure as proof that there is no reason to return to Jesus, remember Peter.
The same Lord who confronted his denial also called him to follow.
But there is another man in Scripture whose story should disturb us just as deeply.
A man who knew the commandments.
A man who appeared morally serious.
A man who came to Jesus with a question about eternal life.
We often call him the rich young ruler.
In Mark 10, he approached Jesus and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life.
He had kept the commandments he mentioned from his youth, according to his own account.
He seemed earnest.
Respectful.
Religiously disciplined.
And then Mark records a detail so beautiful that it is easy to overlook.
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him.” — Mark 10:21 (KJV)
Jesus loved him.
Before the man walked away.
Before the difficult command.
Before the heartbreaking ending.
Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus exposed the attachment that was competing with his devotion to God.
He told the man to sell what he possessed, give to the poor, and follow Him.
This was a specific confrontation of that man's bondage to wealth, not a universal command that every Christian must dispose of every possession.
But the spiritual issue reaches far beyond money.
What happens when Jesus confronts the thing you are unwilling to surrender?
The man's face fell.
He went away grieving.
Because he had great possessions.
He came to Jesus asking about eternal life.
But when Jesus called him to follow, his possessions held his heart.
And this is where the story stops feeling ancient.
Because many of us want Jesus to give us eternal life without disturbing the things we have enthroned in His place.
We want Him to forgive us without changing our habits.
Comfort us without confronting our pride.
Bless our plans without questioning our priorities.
Heal our wounds without asking us to release our bitterness.
Save us from judgment without becoming Lord over our lives.
We want the promises of the kingdom.
But we resist the King.
And the saddest part is that we may know enough Bible verses to justify our resistance.
We can find words that comfort us while avoiding passages that challenge us.
We can build a version of Christianity that never interferes with our favorite sin.
But the real Jesus cannot be reduced to a collection of inspirational sayings.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He gives grace freely.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
And immediately afterward:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10 (KJV)
Do you see the beauty of that order?
We are not saved because we have performed enough good works.
We are saved by grace through faith.
And the grace that saves us also begins transforming how we live.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are the fruit of God's work in those who belong to Christ.
This is why a genuine relationship with Jesus is not measured by flawless performance.
If perfection were the standard, every one of us would stand condemned.
Rather, the life of faith is marked by dependence upon Christ, repentance when we sin, growing obedience, love for God and others, and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
There will be struggles.
There will be tears.
There may be seasons when prayer feels difficult and Scripture seems harder to understand.
A believer can experience weakness, grief, temptation, doubt, and spiritual dryness without those experiences automatically proving that the relationship with God is false.
But we must not confuse struggling against sin with making peace with it.
We must not confuse imperfect obedience with deliberate refusal to follow Christ.
And we must never mistake religious familiarity for saving faith.
James 1:22 says:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” (KJV)
The Greek is piercing:
Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταί
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai.
“But be doers of the word, and not hearers only.”
The word ποιηταί — poiētai refers to doers, people who put something into practice.
James is not teaching that our obedience purchases forgiveness.
He is confronting the self-deception of hearing God's Word without responding to it.
A Bible that never challenges our conduct can become little more than an accessory to our religious identity.
A sermon we applaud but refuse to obey may entertain our conscience without changing our direction.
A verse we post publicly while rejecting its meaning privately can become a witness against our hypocrisy.
And perhaps that is why some of the most dangerous words a Christian can say are:
“I already know that verse.”
Because knowing the words is not the same as receiving their correction.
You may know that God is love.
But are you learning to love the person who is difficult to love?
You may know that God is holy.
But are you bringing your secret compromises into His light?
You may know that God is faithful.
But are you trusting Him when obedience costs you something?
You may know that Jesus forgives.
But have you actually come to Him with the guilt you have been carrying?
You may know that Jesus is Lord.
But whose voice has the final authority over your decisions?
These are not questions meant to turn salvation into an endless exercise in self-suspicion.
They are questions meant to direct our attention away from religious appearances and back toward Christ.
Because the center of Christianity is not our ability to examine ourselves perfectly.
The center is Jesus.
And this brings us to something extraordinary.
In John 17, shortly before His arrest, Jesus prayed to the Father.
He spoke of eternal life.
Not as a vague religious feeling.
Not as merely living forever.
But in profoundly relational terms.
“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” — John 17:3 (KJV)
The Greek phrase is:
ἵνα γινώσκωσιν σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν καὶ ὃν ἀπέστειλας Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν
Hina ginōskōsin se ton monon alēthinon theon kai hon apesteilas Iēsoun Christon.
“That they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent.”
The verb γινώσκωσιν — ginōskōsin, from ginōskō, means “to know.”
In this context, Jesus speaks of knowing the Father and the Son, not merely collecting information about them.
That does not mean biblical truth is unimportant.
Quite the opposite.
We cannot truly know God by inventing a version of Him that suits our preferences.
We know Him through His revelation, supremely in His Son, Jesus Christ.
But that knowledge is meant to lead us into faith, worship, love, trust, and fellowship with Him.
The tragedy is not that someone knows too much Scripture.
The tragedy is that someone can become satisfied with knowing facts about God while refusing to come to Him.
Imagine a child who has memorized every detail of his father's biography.
His birthday.
His favorite meal.
His childhood home.
His achievements.
His habits.
The child can answer every question about his father.
But he never speaks to him.
Never trusts him.
Never comes to him for comfort.
Never listens when his father calls.
Never enjoys his presence.
Would we describe that as a healthy relationship simply because the child knows the facts?
Of course not.
And yet, sometimes we treat our relationship with God as though accurate information alone were the destination.
But the Bible does not merely invite us to know what God has said.
It invites us to know the God who has spoken.
To hear His truth.
To trust His promises.
To receive His Son.
To walk in His ways.
To love Him because He first loved us.
And to discover that the God who knows us completely has made a way for sinners to be reconciled to Him.
That way is Jesus Christ.
Not your church attendance.
Not your biblical vocabulary.
Not your generosity.
Not your ability to inspire people online.
Not even the emotional intensity of your religious experiences.
Jesus.
The Son of God who became flesh.
The sinless Savior who bore our sins.
The crucified Redeemer who died and was buried.
The risen Lord who conquered death.
The only mediator between God and humanity.
The One who said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6 (KJV)
And this is where the Gospel becomes deeply personal.
Because God does not merely offer you better religious information.
He offers reconciliation with Himself through Christ.
The person who has spent years pretending can stop pretending.
The believer who has grown cold can repent and return to wholehearted devotion.
The sinner who has been hiding can confess and seek mercy.
The exhausted Christian can admit weakness and seek renewed strength.
The wounded person can bring pain to the Savior without pretending healing has already happened.
And the person who has never truly trusted Jesus can turn to Him in repentance and faith.
There is no need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
No need to invent tears.
No need to make promises you cannot keep.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come believing that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that you must somehow become impressive enough for God to love you.
It is the announcement that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every failure.
Not after we memorized enough verses.
Not after we became spiritually admirable.
While we were sinners.
That is grace.
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings us to Christ and begins changing us through His Spirit.
The same Jesus who said, “Come unto me,” also said, “Follow me.”
The same Savior who forgives calls us to turn away from sin.
The same Lord who receives the brokenhearted teaches His people to walk in truth.
And His grace is greater than the false choice between religious performance and careless living.
We are called neither to earn His love through perfection nor to presume upon His mercy through deliberate rebellion.
We are called to belong to Him.
So perhaps the question today is not how many Bible verses you know.
Perhaps it is what happens when those verses speak directly to the parts of your life you would rather keep hidden.
When Scripture tells you to forgive, do you begin seeking God's help to release the bitterness?
When Scripture exposes your pride, do you defend yourself or humble yourself?
When Scripture calls you to holiness, do you seek repentance or invent another excuse?
When Scripture tells you that Christ is sufficient, do you begin placing your confidence in Him rather than in your spiritual reputation?
When Scripture tells you that you are loved in Christ, do you receive that truth, or do you continue living as though God's mercy must be purchased by your achievements?
And when Jesus calls you to come to Him…
Do you come?
Not to impress Him.
Not to perform.
Not to bargain.
But to surrender.
Because someday the applause will stop.
The notifications will disappear.
The titles people gave us will mean nothing.
Nobody will be impressed by the number of Christian posts we published.
Our carefully managed image will no longer protect us.
And what will matter is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
That should sober us.
But it should also awaken hope.
Because the invitation to come to Christ is not reserved for people who have already mastered the Christian life.
It is for sinners who need a Savior.
For the proud who need humbling.
For the guilty who need forgiveness.
For the spiritually empty who need life.
For the weary who need rest.
And for those who have confused religious activity with genuine fellowship with God.
Jesus says in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
Notice again those beautiful words.
Come unto Me.
Not merely to another event.
Not merely to another inspirational quotation.
Not merely to another religious performance.
Come to Jesus.
And if something in this article has exposed an uncomfortable truth in your life, do not waste that moment trying to look spiritual.
Speak honestly to God.
Maybe your prayer is:

“Jesus, I have known so much about You, but I have allowed my heart to drift. Forgive me. Expose what I have hidden. Teach me to love Your Word because it reveals who You are. Help me trust You, obey You, and walk with You when nobody is watching. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me what it means to follow You with my whole life. Amen.”
Those words are not a magical formula.
Salvation does not come through reciting a particular prayer.
It comes by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But an honest cry to God can mark the beginning of repentance, renewed surrender, and a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
And perhaps today is the day you stop confusing familiarity with intimacy.
Perhaps today is the day you open your Bible, not simply looking for something to post, but asking God to teach you what is true.
Perhaps today is the day you confess the sin you have been rationalizing.
Perhaps today is the day you seek reconciliation with someone you have wounded.
Perhaps today is the day you return to Christian fellowship after isolating yourself in shame.
Perhaps today is the day you stop running from the One who calls you to come.
And perhaps today, for the first time, you understand why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a crowd of people who merely admire powerful Christian words.
Not to create another place where religious appearances can hide wounded hearts.
But to point people back to Jesus Christ through Scripture, discipleship, repentance, grace, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Because there are people who know the language of Christianity but have never understood the beauty of Christ.
There are believers quietly starving for biblical nourishment while their social media feeds overflow with spiritual noise.
There are parents trying to lead their families toward God while struggling with their own questions.
There are young people who have heard religious rules but have rarely encountered a clear explanation of the Gospel.
There are exhausted Christians who need sound teaching, genuine encouragement, and reminders that growth in Christ is a lifelong journey.
That is why sharing biblical truth matters.
Not because every share will change a life.
Not because a viral post guarantees a conversion.
But because God can use the faithful communication of His Word to bring people face-to-face with the truth about Jesus.
And if this article reached a part of your heart you have been avoiding, consider doing something meaningful with that conviction.
Don't let it become another emotional moment that disappears beneath the next notification.
You do not need to reveal private sins or painful details publicly. But if you are comfortable, tell us what Scripture has been teaching you about following Jesus.
Maybe you have been struggling to pray.
Maybe you are learning to forgive.
Maybe you have recently returned to Christ after a season of spiritual coldness.
Maybe you are discovering that knowing Jesus is more beautiful than simply appearing religious.
Your testimony may encourage someone who believes they are the only person struggling.
And if you need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You don't have to explain everything.
You are not alone in needing God's grace.
Then think of one person who needs to hear this.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to accuse of being a hypocrite.
Someone you genuinely love.
A brother.
A sister.
A friend who has grown distant from God.
A family member who is searching for truth.
A believer who knows Scripture but has become spiritually exhausted.
Because sharing the Gospel is not about winning attention.
It is about faithfully pointing people toward Christ.
Not as another item in a collection of religious posts, but as something to return to when your spiritual life begins to feel like performance rather than fellowship with God.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, grow in understanding, strengthen their walk with Jesus, and become more firmly rooted in biblical truth.
And I want to speak personally to those who believe in this mission.
Producing, maintaining, and expanding Christian teaching resources requires time, work, and practical support.
It is one practical way to participate in the mission.
And there is something important I want you to understand.
You do not have to give money to earn His favor.
You do not have to purchase access to His grace.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ, never a benefit bought through financial support.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Christian generosity should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
It can complement their regular tithes and offerings, while remembering that responsibilities toward their local church, family, and those in need should not be neglected.
It is a voluntary contribution toward sharing the message of the God who has already given us so much in Christ.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encouragement in daily life, or thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to help make Scripture-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
To help sustain work that points beyond itself.
To help others discover the grace of Jesus Christ.
To be part of a mission where the message matters more than the platform.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
The free resources remain an invitation to pursue a deeper knowledge of God's Word.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God, and they do not determine whether you belong in this community.
A heartfelt prayer matters.
A faithful share matters.
An encouraging comment matters.
A quiet conversation about Jesus with someone who is searching for hope matters.
And above all, knowing and following Christ matters.
Because when all is said and done, Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Jesus can.
A book cannot forgive your sins.
Jesus can.
A Christian T-shirt cannot make you righteous.
Jesus can.
A thousand religious posts cannot reconcile you to God.
Only the saving work of Jesus Christ can do that.
And if this ministry ever becomes more important to you than the Lord it exists to proclaim, something has gone wrong.
Our mission must always lead back to Him.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who restored Peter.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls people to repentance and faith.
The One who can take a life stained by shame, rebellion, pride, regret, and failure and make it a testimony of undeserved grace.
That is the heart of our message.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the sin did not matter.
Not because the consequences always disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save, and His grace can accomplish what human effort never could.
He can forgive the guilty.
Humble the proud.
Restore the fallen.
Transform the rebellious.
Give hope to the brokenhearted.
And make new creations of those who belong to Him.
As 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, open your Bible.
Read slowly.
Read honestly.
Read prayerfully.
And when you encounter the words of Jesus, don't merely ask whether you can remember them.
Ask whether you believe Him.
Ask whether you are trusting Him.
Ask whether your life is being shaped by His truth.
And when His Word reveals something painful, don't run from Him in shame.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because the goal was never to become someone who could quote the most verses while remaining distant from the Savior.
The goal is to know the true and living God through Jesus Christ, to be reconciled to Him by grace, and to grow in love and obedience through the power of His Spirit.
One day, your Bible will be closed for the last time.
Your final post will already have been published.
Your last earthly conversation will have ended.
And the reputation you worked so hard to protect will no longer be able to speak for you.
But the question of whether you belong to Christ will remain.
So don't settle for knowing the words while refusing the One to whom they point.
Don't spend your whole life studying the invitation while never responding to it.
Don't confuse the appearance of faith with faith itself.
And don't forget that the Savior who calls you to come is the very Savior who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
The greatest tragedy would be to know His words by heart, yet never give your heart to the One those words reveal.
